title: Product of Array Except Self — prefix × suffix product, no division.
shortTitle: Product of Array Except Self — Prefix × Suffix, No Division

s1_definition.profdef: The Product of Array Except Self problem asks you to produce, for each position, the product of every other element, without using division. The linear solution computes for each position the product of all elements to its left, called the prefix product, and the product of all elements to its right, called the suffix product, and multiplies them. Done in two passes with the output array also serving as storage, it runs in linear time and uses constant extra space beyond the output.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India computes, for each of several contributing factors to a portfolio growth multiplier, the combined effect of all the other factors, so it can see how the portfolio would grow if one factor were removed. The trick without dividing is to sweep left to right building up the running product of everything before each factor, then sweep right to left building up the running product of everything after it, and multiply the two sweeps at each position. Each factor's answer is the product of all the others.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each index, multiply the product of everything to the left by the product of everything to the right, using two sweeps and no division.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Product of Array Except Self problem asks you to produce, for each position, the product of every other element, without using division. The linear solution computes for each position the product of all elements to its left, called the prefix product, and the product of all elements to its right, called the suffix product, and multiplies them. Done in two passes with the output array also serving as storage, it runs in linear time and uses constant extra space beyond the output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India computes, for each of several contributing factors to a portfolio growth multiplier, the combined effect of all the other factors, so it can see how the portfolio would grow if one factor were removed. The trick without dividing is to sweep left to right building up the running product of everything before each factor, then sweep right to left building up the running product of everything after it, and multiply the two sweeps at each position. Each factor's answer is the product of all the others.

**One line to remember:** For each index, multiply the product of everything to the left by the product of everything to the right, using two sweeps and no division.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive idea is to compute the total product of all elements and then divide by each element. That is linear but it is forbidden here, and for good reason: division fails when any element is zero, because you cannot divide by zero, and handling zeros turns into an ugly special case. The prefix-suffix method avoids division entirely and handles zeros naturally.

The method uses two logical passes. In the first pass you move left to right and fill each output position with the product of all elements strictly to its left; you keep a running prefix product that starts at the multiplicative identity, one, and before writing you store the current running product, then multiply the running product by the current element for the next position. After this pass, output at position i holds the product of everything before i.

In the second pass you move right to left with a running suffix product, also starting at one. At each position you multiply the value already in the output, which is the prefix product, by the running suffix product, then multiply the running suffix by the current element for the next position. After this pass, each output position holds prefix times suffix, which is the product of every element except the one at that position.

A senior point about space is that using the output array to hold the prefix products and then multiplying in the suffix on the fly means you do not need a separate suffix array, so the extra space is constant beyond the required output. The problem usually says the output does not count toward extra space, so this is the optimal constant-space linear-time solution.

Another senior point is the zero handling that comes for free. If exactly one element is zero, only that position gets a non-zero answer and all others become zero, which the prefix-suffix method produces correctly without any special branch. If two or more elements are zero, every position's answer is zero, also handled naturally. The division approach would need explicit counting of zeros to get these right, which is error-prone.

For finance I use BigDecimal to keep the products exact, multiplying with the BigDecimal multiply method, because growth multipliers and factor products must not drift due to floating-point rounding. I also note overflow: with primitive int or long the products can overflow quickly, so BigDecimal is doubly justified here.

A small finance-domain example: first pass `out[i] = prefix; prefix = prefix.multiply(a[i]);` left to right, then second pass `out[i] = out[i].multiply(suffix); suffix = suffix.multiply(a[i]);` right to left, yielding each factor's all-others product.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models Rajesh's portfolio growth as a product of several independent factor multipliers, and the analytics team wants, for each factor, the combined multiplier of all the other factors, to run a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. They must not use division, because some factors can be exactly one or even zero in stress scenarios, and dividing would be fragile. Computing each leave-one-out product with prefix and suffix sweeps is exactly this.

This is exactly how product-except-self works in Java — a left sweep builds the product before each factor and a right sweep multiplies in the product after it.

Problem 2 — The multipliers are precise BigDecimal values and can include a zero in a stress scenario, so the method must handle zeros naturally without a division special case, and it must keep the arithmetic exact. This shows why the prefix-suffix approach, combined with BigDecimal, is the right tool.

What the code will do: a `SensitivityAnalyzer` with `productExceptSelf(BigDecimal[] factors)` using two sweeps and the output array for prefix storage, no division. The demo runs a leave-one-out analysis on Rajesh's factor multipliers including a zero stress case.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the factor multipliers are `2, 3, 4, 5`.

Step 1: Pass one, left to right, prefix starts at one. At index zero we write prefix one into output, then multiply prefix by `2` to get `2`. At index one we write `2`, then prefix becomes `2 * 3 = 6`.

Step 2: At index two we write `6`, then prefix becomes `6 * 4 = 24`. At index three we write `24`, then prefix becomes `24 * 5 = 120`. After pass one the output holds the products before each position: `1, 2, 6, 24`.

Step 3: Pass two, right to left, suffix starts at one. At index three we multiply the stored `24` by suffix one to get `24`, then suffix becomes `1 * 5 = 5`.

Step 4: At index two we multiply the stored `6` by suffix `5` to get `30`, then suffix becomes `5 * 4 = 20`. At index one we multiply the stored `2` by suffix `20` to get `40`, then suffix becomes `20 * 3 = 60`.

Step 5: At index zero we multiply the stored `1` by suffix `60` to get `60`, then suffix becomes `60 * 2 = 120`. The output is now `60, 40, 30, 24`, each being the product of all other factors, computed with no division and only the output array plus two running products.

Step 6: For the stressed input with a zero at index one, the prefix-suffix method naturally gives `0, 40, 0, 0`, because every position except the zero includes the zero factor in either its prefix or its suffix, while the zero's own position is the product of the non-zero others. No special zero handling was needed.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z INFO Leave-one-out products: [60, 40, 30, 24]
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z INFO Normal factors [2, 3, 4, 5] → [60, 40, 30, 24]
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z INFO Leave-one-out products: [0, 40, 0, 0]
2026-10-26T17:50:00Z INFO Stressed factors [2, 0, 4, 5] → [0, 40, 0, 0]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Product of Array Except Self asks for, at each position, the product of every other element, without division. I solve it with prefix and suffix products. In a left-to-right pass I fill each output position with the product of everything before it, carrying a running prefix product. In a right-to-left pass I multiply each output by a running suffix product, the product of everything after it. Prefix times suffix at each position is the product of all elements except that one.

The reason division is banned is sound: dividing the total product by each element breaks when any element is zero and forces an ugly zero-counting special case. The prefix-suffix method sidesteps that completely, and it handles zeros for free: one zero makes every position zero except the zero's own position, and two or more zeros make everything zero, all without a special branch.

On space, I reuse the output array to hold the prefix products and multiply the suffix in on the fly, so I need no separate suffix array, giving constant extra space beyond the required output, which is the optimal linear-time solution. For finance I use BigDecimal so the products stay exact and do not drift with floating-point rounding, and because primitive products would overflow quickly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this for a leave-one-out sensitivity analysis on Rajesh's portfolio, modelling growth as a product of factor multipliers and computing, for each factor, the combined multiplier of all the others, including stress scenarios where a factor is zero. Avoiding division kept it robust, and BigDecimal kept it exact. Explaining the two-sweep method, why division is avoided, and the natural zero handling shows the interviewer that I know the optimal technique and why it is designed that way.
